13900-collected-poems-1897-1907-by-henry:
Henry Newbolt collected his poems from 1897 to 1907 in this volume, dedicated to Thomas Hardy. Drake's Drum opens the book, with Drake asleep in his hammock a thousand miles away, dreaming of Plymouth Hoe. Sailor lads dance, shore lights flash, and night tides dash in the famous refrain. Other poems follow fleets, soldiers, and English history.

Newbolt writes stirring verse on duty, empire, and the sea. A later poem watches the Straits open wide, with hearts dancing like the sea as the French sail for Martinique. The collection captures Edwardian patriotic poetry at its peak. Modern readers may find its imperial tone dated, yet its music endures. It remains Newbolt's best-known gathering.
14244-the-romance-of-tristan-and-iseult:
Joseph Bédier retold the romance of Tristan and Iseult from the best French sources, and H. Belloc rendered it into English in 1913. Crowned by the French Academy, the tale opens with Tristan's childhood, the Morholt out of Ireland, and the quest for the lady with hair of gold. A philtre binds the lovers, and the tall pine tree, the discovery, and the chantry leap follow.

Exile and ordeal deepen the story. In the wood of Morois, Ogrin the hermit shelters the pair, while Brangien devises subtle ruses to save them. Iseult dreams of scythes and traps cutting her knees, and blood upon the ground. King Mark, pressed by barons, exiles Tristan, then drives the barons themselves from his land when they fall silent. Madness, a second Iseult of the White Hands, and death close the romance. Love and fate, told simply, still overwhelm.
17178-westerfelt:
Will N. Harben's 1901 novel opens at a quilting in a mountain home, where two sisters and their neighbors sew a bright, varicolored square and gossip the day away. Mrs. Slogan, childless and past sixty, praises the quilt as the prettiest yet, while her softer sister Mrs. Dawson irons out its wrinkles. The sun sets behind the mountain as the workers leave by field and wood paths.

From this homely start Harben builds a southern mountain tale of kin, pride, and love, told in dialect speech and close home detail. The quilting scene sets the book's tone: plain folk, sharp talk, and strong feeling under a quiet roof. Readers who like regional novels will enjoy its slow, vivid opening and its mountain world.
22352-american-boy-s-life-of-theodore-ro:
Edward Stratemeyer's American Boys' Life of Theodore Roosevelt came out in 1904. It told the president's life for young readers. A plate shows Colonel Roosevelt at San Juan Hill, his famous battle.

Stratemeyer had already written an American boys' life of William McKinley. He also produced the Old Glory and Pan-American series for boys. This volume fits that pattern of patriotic biography. Boys were offered Roosevelt as soldier, leader, and example. The book shows how a sitting president was packaged as a hero for youth. Readers today can study both Roosevelt's image and the boys' book trade at once.
23810-at-fault:
Kate Chopin's At Fault opens on a Louisiana plantation of four thousand acres, left unencumbered to Thérèse Lafirme. When her husband Jérôme dies suddenly, neighbors watch with indolent interest, expecting some folly from a handsome, inconsolable, childless Creole widow of thirty.

The folly fails to appear. Thérèse follows her husband's methods so successfully that the only wonder is her competence. Around her move Melicent, Fanny, and the household of Place-du-Bois, through pine woods, pirogues, and painful disclosures. Chopin's novel studies a widow's independence, a sister's talk, and the slow, fateful working of fault and forgiveness.
29021-the-fairy-tales-of-charles-perraul:
Charles Perrault's fairy tales appear here in the edition illustrated by Harry Clarke, with an introduction by Thomas Bodkin, first published by Harrap in London in August 1922. The contents run from Little Red Riding-Hood and The Fairy through Blue Beard and The Sleeping Beauty in the Wood to The Master Cat, or Puss in Boots. Cinderilla, Riquet with the Tuft, Little Thumb, and Donkey-Skin follow.

Clarke's pictures, including Cinderilla and her prince as frontispiece, dress the old tales in rich, strange art. Bodkin's introduction sets Perrault's stories in their French classic form. Readers get the best-known fairy tales of Europe in a handsome edition, suited to reading aloud and to keeping, with pictures that match the tales' wonder and menace.
29312-camping-with-president-roosevelt:
John Burroughs published this account in 1906, reprinted from The Atlantic Monthly of May 1906, of his camping trip to Yellowstone Park with President Theodore Roosevelt in the spring of 1903. Burroughs had promised friends to write up his impressions of the president and the park, though he was slow to get around to it. Roosevelt himself, Burroughs jokes, wrote his account nearly two years earlier from the leisure of the White House.

Chapters cover the president's interest in natural history, his love of animals, meeting the people, cowboy friends, ranch life, and the Bad Lands and bad men. Readers get a naturalist's portrait of a president outdoors, warm and observant, from the days when Yellowstone itself was still a wild frontier.
4252-theodore-roosevelt:
Edmund Lester Pearson wrote this short life of Theodore Roosevelt for the True Stories of Great Americans series. Macmillan published it in 1920, a year after Roosevelt's death. Pearson drew on Roosevelt's own writings for the story. He also drew on William Roscoe Thayer's intimate biography.

The chapters trace a path from a sickly boy to soldier, governor, and president. They cover his ranching years and his service in the Spanish-American War. They cover his White House years and his later travels and writing. Written close to its subject's lifetime, the book gives young readers a clear, admiring outline.
6075-miss-gibbie-gault:
Kate Langley Bosher, author of Mary Cary, opens Miss Gibbie Gault with the Needlework Guild, meeting Thursdays at eleven, this time with Mrs. Tate for the last gathering before summer adjournment. Mrs. Pryor, the president, has personally requested a large attendance, and gossip, the guild's true business, hums along.

Chapters follow the views of Miss Gibbie, apple-blossom land, a council chamber, Mary Cary speaking, midnight, Peggy and her party, and a forgotten engagement. A bargain, a grateful convalescent, a testimony party, and a surrender follow. Bosher writes warm small-town comedy, where talk shapes fates.
7360-the-tryal-of-william-penn-william-m:
The Tryal of William Penn and William Mead for causing a tumult records the Old Bailey sessions of September 1, 3, 4, and 5, 1670. It was done by themselves and transcribed from the Compleat Collection of State Tryals first published in 1719, edited by Don Seitz. Seitz dedicates the volume to the memory of Thomas Jefferson, which needs frequent refreshing. His foreword praises Penn, the Quaker, for coming nearer than any other human being to establishing liberty, equality, and fraternity as a living ideal.

Penn's courtroom stand for conscience and jury freedom gives the trial its lasting fame. The old record lets readers hear the clash of judge, jury, and prisoner in its own words. This text preserves a founding moment of religious liberty and trial by jury.
9631-waltoniana-inedited-remains-in-vers:
Richard Herne Shepherd edited Waltoniana in 1878, gathering unprinted remains of Izaak Walton, author of The Compleat Angler. The book spans 1633 to 1673, from an elegy on Dr. Donne to dedications, prefaces, and letters. Pieces include lines on Donne's portrait, verses for a merchants' map, and a preface to Quarles. An epitaph for Walton's second wife Anne Ken also appears.

Shepherd's notes and preface place each scrap in Walton's long life among poets and divines. The remains show Walton as friend, churchman, and angler, not just a single book's author. A reader gets a rare, intimate Walton, in small pieces that light up seventeenth-century English letters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anhalt:
Anhalt is a Vicariate Apostolic covering the German Duchy of Anhalt, 860 square miles. On 1 December 1905 it contained 328,029 inhabitants, mostly Protestants, with 13,493 Catholics. The Bishop of Paderborn, as vicar apostolic, names its pastors. There are four parishes, Dessau, Bernburg, Coethen, and Zerbst, plus three missions.

The Grey Nuns from Breslau, the only order in Anhalt, run visiting-nurse establishments in Dessau and Coethen, plus a kindergarten and a school in Coethen. The public schools are state-directed, yet the Church maintains sixteen private schools. Before the Reformation, Anhalt belonged to the bishoprics of Meissen, Brandenburg, and Merseburg. The few Catholics remaining after those dioceses fell received little attention until 1622. In 1719 the Saxon Franciscans established a mission in Dessau, given a chapel in 1805. Missions followed at Zerbst and Coethen. Duke Ferdinand of Coethen and his wife became Catholics at Paris in 1825 and founded a Coethen congregation, raised to a parish in 1826.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-const:
Charles Constance Cesar Joseph Mattheu d'Agoult was a French prelate born at Grenoble in 1747 and dead at Paris in 1824. He trained at the Seminary of St. Sulpice in Paris. He became Bishop of Pamiers in 1787. During the Revolution he emigrated, returning to France only after surrendering his bishopric.

His writings were political and financial rather than theological. They include a project for a national bank in 1815 with an explanatory follow-up in 1816. A letter to a Jacobin reflects on the English constitution and the royal charter. A conversation with E. Burke on the interests of Europe's powers appeared in 1814. Four such works are listed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-perra:
An entry on Charles Perrault, the French writer whose fairy tales made him famous. Born in Paris in 1628, he practised law briefly, then became chief clerk in the king's buildings office in 1664. He suggested the Louvre colonnade to his architect brother Claude and persuaded Colbert to fund pensions for writers and scholars. He helped create the Academy of Sciences and served as lifelong secretary of the Academy of Inscriptions.

Elected to the French Academy in 1671, Perrault opened its meetings to the public. His preface to Le siècle de Louis le Grand and his Parallèle des Anciens et des Modernes launched the quarrel of Ancients and Moderns. There he championed modern writers against Boileau and Bossuet. All of it was outshone by his Contes de ma Mère l'Oye of 1697, the Mother Goose tales, retold with a skill that gave them lasting popularity. He died in 1703.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-raymb:
An entry on Charles Raymbault, a French Jesuit missionary and the first Jesuit to die in Canada. Born in France in 1602, he entered the Society of Jesus at Rouen in 1621. He served as procurator, or business manager, of the Canadian mission before being called to Quebec in 1637. In 1640 he was sent with Father Pijart to follow wandering tribes visiting the Hurons, chiefly Nipissings and Algonquins east and north of Lake Huron.

That mission brought harder conditions than work among the Hurons or the Tobacco Nation, but Jesuit generosity soon bore fruit. When the Sauteux asked for priests in 1641, Raymbault went with the future martyr Jogues as far as Sault Ste. Marie, seeking both converts and the fabled passage to the Western Sea. Worn out by fatigue on his return, he was carried to Quebec, where he died in 1643 and was buried beside Champlain, the colony's founder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-perrau:
Claude Perrault, born at Paris in 1613 and dead there in 1688, built the main eastern facade of the Louvre, known as the Colonnade. He succeeded in medicine and anatomy, in architecture, and as an author, though his talent won him much enmity, especially in architecture. As physician and physicist he took his doctorate at the University of Paris. He joined the Academy of Sciences at its founding in 1666 and repeatedly won prizes for physics and chemistry.

Colbert had him translate Vitruvius, and the work fired his enthusiasm for architecture. His Vitruvius with commentary and tables appeared in 1673, with an epitome in 1674. His Ordering of the Five Kinds of Columns followed in 1683. His triumphal arch design for the Rue Saint-Antoine, preferred to Lebrun's and Leveau's, was only partly built in stone. In the Louvre colonnade competition he beat all rivals, even Bernini, and the work occupied him from 1665 to 1680.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-hunolt:
Franz Hunolt, born at Siegen on 31 March 1691 and dead at Trier on 12 September 1746, was the best-loved German preacher of the early eighteenth century. His name appears in Jesuit catalogues as Humold, Hunoldt, and usually Hunolt. At nine he entered his town's Jesuit college, at fifteen studied philosophy at Cologne, took his master of arts, and entered the Society of Jesus there on 18 May. After a two-year novitiate at Trier and a year at Geyst preparing to teach, he taught at Cologne and Aachen gymnasiums to his superiors' complete satisfaction. He directed the junior sodality and showed remarkable oratorical gifts.

After four years of theology and holy orders, he spent most of his third probation year giving popular missions, so great was his preaching fame. He then took the logic chair at Coblenz and made his profession on 15 August 1724.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-barthe:
George-Barthélemy Faribault, a Quebec archaeologist born in 1789, gave his leisure and fortune to Canada's past. Cousin of the founder of Faribault, Minnesota, he schooled himself for law after a Scotch veteran's classroom. He joined the bar in 1811 and fought as a militiaman against the American invasion of 1812. In 1822 he entered the civil service, rising to assistant clerk of the Assembly by 1832.

Faribault spent every free hour gathering Canadian books and papers, and his fine haul of 1,700 rarities burned with Montreal's Parliament House in 1849. Undaunted, he built a second collection, later left to Laval University. His Catalogue of Works on American history, issued at Quebec in 1837, still ranks among the best, and in 1859 he raised Montcalm's long-planned memorial tablet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-victor-:
Orphaned at eight, Henri Victor Regnault worked as a drapery clerk in Paris while studying in spare hours until he entered the École Polytechnique in 1830. He moved from organic chemistry, where he built new compounds by substituting chlorine for hydrogen, into physics. In 1843 the French government charged him with measuring the properties of steam for engineers. Published in 1847, those results won him the Rumford Medal and the post of Chief Engineer of Mines.

Regnault's reputation rests on exact measurement: specific heats of solids, liquids, and gases, vapour tensions, latent heats, expansion coefficients, and a correction to Mariotte's law of gases. Two laws on the specific heat of gases bear his name, and his tables became standards for engineers and chemists. Directing the Sèvres porcelain works from 1852, he lost laboratory, instruments, and papers in the Franco-German War, a blow compounded by his son's death and a stroke in 1873.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacob-arcadel:
Jacob Arcadelt was a noted musician born in Holland around 1500. He died probably at Paris between 1570 and 1575. He grew up under Josquin and the Belgian school. He began as a singer at Florence's court. In 1539 he went to Rome. He became singing master of St Peter's boys' choir. The next year he joined the papal choir as a singer. He stayed there until 1549.

In 1555 Cardinal Charles of Lorraine engaged his services. Arcadelt followed him to Paris and likely stayed there until death. He was known then as regius musicus, or court musician. Most of his many works were published. Foremost are six books of five-voice madrigals, issued at Venice from 1538 to 1556. Each book holds at least forty pieces. The entry presents a Franco-Flemish master of the madrigal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste Faribault, a trader and early settler of Minnesota, was born in Lower Canada in 1774 and died at Faribault, Minnesota, in 1860. His father, a Paris lawyer turned Canadian notary, had served the French army in Canada. After schooling and shop work at Quebec, the son joined the Northwest Fur Company.

From Mackinac in 1798 Faribault traded for a decade with Potawatomi, Dakota, and Sioux peoples along the Des Moines and Minnesota rivers. He settled at Prairie du Chien in 1809, trading on his own account and swapping lead with Julien Dubuque. Refusing to join the English in the War of 1812 cost him jail and his goods, yet he stayed and helped found a frontier town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-bertrand:
Léon Foucault, a French physicist born in Paris in 1819 and dead there in 1868. He showed mechanical genius as a boy, building a boat, a telegraph, and a working steam engine. He quit medicine, unable to bear blood, and worked as preparator for Donné's microscopy course, patching his thin maths training as he went.

In 1845 Foucault took charge of science coverage at the Journal des Débats, won the Royal Society's Copley Medal in 1850, and in 1855 became physicist of the Paris Observatory. His turning mirror settled light's speed in different media and overturned the particle theory of light. His pendulum, proving Earth's spin, made his name known far beyond laboratories.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-and-abb:
Fontevrault, a double monastery founded by Robert d'Arbrissel near the end of 1100, placed monks and nuns under an abbess in a wooded valley near the Loire. Its rule drew on John's words Behold thy Mother, but practical sense also counted: able nuns, not the feeble brethren around Robert, could govern.

The long line of capable abbesses justified the choice, and Fontevrault led the double orders before Gilbertines and Bridgettines copied its form. The entry compares their rules, traces the abbey's lands, prisons, and royal burials, and follows it to suppression in the Revolution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-gibaul:
Pierre Gibault was a Canadian missionary and patriot priest of Illinois, born at Montreal in 1737. Educated at Quebec Seminary and ordained on 19 March 1768, Bishop Briand sent him as vicar-general to Illinois. In July he reached Michilimackinac, spent a week serving Catholics long without a priest, and by September settled at Kaskaskia, later living at Ste. Genevieve, Vincennes, and Cahokia.

At Vincennes in February 1770 he found religion deplorable, converted a Presbyterian family in two months, revived Catholic practice, and that year blessed the little wooden chapel at Paincourt, today's St. Louis. Long the only priest in Illinois and Indiana, he swayed Kaskaskia and Cahokia to submit to George Rogers Clark in 1778 and swear allegiance to Virginia. As Clark's volunteer agent he then won Vincennes to the American cause. In 1791 he retired beyond the Mississippi. He died at New Madrid about 1804.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-joseph:
Pierre-Joseph Desault rose from a poor boyhood in Franche-Comté to become the leading surgeon of Paris in his day. He was born at Magny-Vernois in 1744 and schooled by Jesuits. He left priestly studies for medicine and learned from a village barber-surgeon. He opened his own anatomy school in Paris in 1766 while still under twenty.

His hands-on teaching drew three hundred pupils. He went on to head surgery at the Charity Hospital and the Hôtel-Dieu. He founded a school of clinical surgery that drew students from far afield. His writings covered operations and fractures and dislocations, and he died from pneumonia in 1795 after a brief imprisonment during the Revolution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pontifical-in:
A Pontifical Indult is a general faculty, or permission, granted by the Holy See to bishops and others to do something the common law does not allow. General needs, peculiar local conditions, and the impossibility of applying to Rome case by case justify such concessions. They run for a set term of three, five, or ten years, or for a set number of cases.

Indults are personal, to be used by the bishop himself or his vicar-general unless he may pass them on, and they differ from dispensations, which cover one particular case only. In a wider sense indult means any privilege, grace, or favour. The entry lists examples. They run from the Lenten indult and an indult of secularisation to leave a religious order, to an indult for a private oratory or a privileged altar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salt:
Salt, used since ancient times to season food and keep things from rotting, early gained a sacred character. Elisha sweetened a well's waters with it, eastern peoples rubbed it on a newborn child's skin, and strewing it on land dedicated the ground to the gods. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia moves from Scripture through Jewish law to the Roman Rite.

Jewish sacrifices and the loaves of proposition required salt, and in Matthew's Gospel salt stands for wisdom, perhaps once with a power against evil. In church use, which belongs only to the Roman Rite, two kinds appear. Baptismal salt, cleansed and blessed with exorcisms and prayers, is given to the catechumen before entering church. Blessed salt serves other rites. A canon of Carthage suggests catechumens received it several times a year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-william-of:
William of Ebelholt, also called William of Paris and of the Paraclete, reformed Danish religious life from a Paris canonry. Schooled by his uncle Hugh, forty-second abbot of St-Germain-des-Prés, he was ordained subdeacon and given a canonry at Ste-Geneviève-du-Mont. His exemplary life displeased his fellow canons, who slandered him to block his diaconate from Paris's bishop.

He obtained the order from Senlis's bishop through his uncle, and was presented to the little priory of Epinay. In 1148 Eugene III replaced Ste-Geneviève's secular canons with regular canons from St Victor, and William joined the new community as sub-prior. There he defended regular observance against an irregularly appointed prior, winning papal support. Sent to Denmark, he became abbot of Ebelholt, dying there on Easter Sunday 1203.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-perau:
William Perault was a French Dominican writer and preacher mistaken for Archbishop of Lyons. Born at Perault in France, he died at Lyons on a disputed date, some placing it before 1260, others about 1270 or 1275. He studied at Paris, where preaching, perhaps by Jordan of Saxony, drew him to the Dominicans. Custom sent him to Lyons convent for a life both contemplative and active, famed for writings, preaching, and virtue.

For ten years Perault discharged every episcopal task for Lyons during its vacancy, chosen by Philip of Savoy, who held the archbishop's title from 1245 to 1267 without orders. Hence men called Perault bishop, and a later hand added the title to his books, though Gerson, Echard, and Hurter insist he never held the see. His works include the Summa on virtues and vices, sermons on seasons and saints, a guide for religious, and a rule for princes partly by Aquinas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-xavier-barbie:
Xavier Barbier de Montault was a French archaeologist and liturgist of vast learning. Born at Loudun in 1830, he died at Blaslay in 1901. From a noble family, he was entrusted at eight to his great-uncle, Bishop Montault des Isles of Angers. He read theology at Saint Sulpice, then theology and archaeology at Rome's Sapienza. Ill health sent him home in 1857 as historiographer of Angers diocese, where he mined archives, studied inscriptions, and founded a museum.

A Roman stay from 1861 to 1875 deepened his liturgy lore, served bishops as consultor, and set him as theologian to Bishop Desflèches at the Vatican Council. His first study appeared in 1851 in Annales Archéologiques, and Didron charged him with its index. He poured articles into Revue de l'Art Chrétien until 1903, and in 1889 began reprinting his works, planning sixty volumes but reaching sixteen, prized more for erudition than edge.
doe-osti-17010319-development-of-integra: Hunting the best algae for biofuel got its DOE field report, and this text covers the DISCOVR screening and cultivar work. Scientists learn which strains won and why. Pond scum's energy dream gets its data. The screening was recorded. The strains were ranked.
doe-osti-17076359-status-on-ornl-activit: Molten salt creeping where it shouldn't got its ORNL status, and this report covers intrusion and wetting studies. The pages track the salt's sneaky spread. The reactor designers get their warning. The status was ORNL's. The spread was sneaky. The studies were wetting.
doe-osti-2588544-comstock-measure-docume: ComStock's rooftop solar got documented, and this DOE text covers photovoltaics with 40 percent coverage. The pages detail the measure. The building modelers get their reference. The coverage was 40 percent rooftop. The measure was photovoltaic. The reference was modeler. The doc was DOE's.
doe-osti-2997593-summary-of-savannah-riv: Savannah River's FY24 salt waste got summarized, and this DOE report covers the qualification data. The pages detail the findings. The waste processors get their numbers. The year was FY24. The data were qualification. The processors got numbers. The findings were detailed.
doe-osti-2998825-property-measurements-o: Molten fluoride salts got their properties, and this DOE report measures LiF-NaF-KF with dopants. The pages detail the corrosion product data. The reactor chemists get their numbers. The salts were LiF-NaF-KF. The oxygen was doped. The chemists got numbers.
doe-osti-3002984-frequency-and-time-mult: Multiphoton states got multiplexed, and this DOE text covers frequency and time methods. The pages detail the generation findings. The quantum folks get their method. The states were multiphoton. The method was quantum. The generation was state. The method was photon.
doe-osti-3014774-conjugate-heat-transfer: Salt pins got heat-transferred, and this DOE text models the stable reactor safety. The pages detail the conjugate findings. The reactor folks get their data. The pins were salt-filled fuel. The data were reactor. The analysis was safety.
doe-osti-3029103-functional-characteriza: Duckweed got glycosyltransferase-characterized, and this DOE text enables predictive biology. The pages detail the functional findings. The bio folks get their data. The biology was predictive. The data were bio. The duckweed were biology. The predictive were biology. The data were DOE.
doe-osti-3366049-final-scientific-techni: Lithium got simultaneously extracted, and this DOE final reports thin-film deposition. The pages detail the scientific findings. The chemists get their closeout. The metal was lithium. The closeout was chemist. The deposition were thin-film. The lithium were metal.
doe-osti-3419449-suli-report-development: Molten salt got loop-developed, and this DOE SULI covers in-situ spectroscopy. The pages detail the development findings. The chemists get their data. The report was circulation. The data were chemist. The SULI were loop. The spectroscopy were in-situ.
doe-osti-3683869-fy26-progress-on-demons: Core expansion got FY26-multiphysicsed, and this DOE progress covers steady state modeling. The pages detail the progress findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The demonstration was capability. The data were nuclear. The FY26 were progress. The radial were expansion.
doe-osti-3684036-zprd-database-zppr-15-m: ZPRD got Monte-Carlo-resulted, and this DOE database covers ZPPR-15 results. The pages detail the database findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The results were Monte Carlo. The data were nuclear. The ZPPR-15 were database. The Carlo were Monte.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CakebreadWalt_C:
Jack White, the Fort Worth photo analyst who spent decades on the Kennedy evidence, wrote this piece on a ballistics claim by a California researcher, Walt Cakebread. Its target is the stretcher bullet theory, part of the single-bullet account at the center of the Warren Report.

The single-bullet theory holds that one bullet wounded both Kennedy and Governor Connally, and the nearly pristine bullet found on a Parkland stretcher is its most contested exhibit. Cakebread's discovery, as White presents it, says that story may be a lie. The piece is assassination-research literature in its native form: an attack on one exhibit, argued in detail.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va:
Jeffrey T. Richelson edited this briefing book, number 590, published in May 2017. It highlights the Archive's Cyber Vault collection by naming more than forty primary sources that every cyber student needs. The list works as a guided entry point into a large archive.

Primary sources on cyber history are scattered across agencies and decades. A curated set of forty-odd documents gives a newcomer the founding papers in one place: early warnings, key decisions, and program records. Teachers and students can use the selection as a syllabus core, then follow its threads into the wider Cyber Vault holdings.
miss-gibbie-gault:
Kate Langley Bosher, the author of Mary Cary, set this novel in a small Southern town. Its first chapter convenes the Guild of Gossips. Miss Gibbie's views, announced in chapter two, drive the talk of the town. Mary Cary herself speaks in later chapters and puzzles over events.

Chapters follow Peggy and her party, a bargain, and a grateful convalescent. A forgotten engagement, a testimony party, and a sudden change build the complications. The ending chapters are titled The Surrender and A Tie That Binds. Bosher writes warmly about a formidable spinster whose sharp tongue hides a generous heart.
nasa-tm-19680006180-semiconductor-switch:
James Vrancik, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, weighed a new kind of electrical switch for spacecraft. His subject is semiconductor switches for alternating-current power in aerospace use. Unlike mechanical switches, these have no moving parts to wear or bounce.

Vrancik studied several static switches built from different devices. He tracked power loss, distortion, leakage, and heat effects in each. The promised gains are high reliability, long life, and resistance to shock and vibration. His team designed and built a breadboard three-phase switch for space use. They tested it starting a fuel pump motor, and found its power loss small.
nasa-tm-19680007863-polarization-measure:
Donald F. Heath, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, measured the day glow of the high air in January 1968. He watched light from oxygen atoms and nitrogen in the far ultraviolet. He checked both how bright the glow was and whether its light waves lined up in one plane.

They did not line up at all, for either the oxygen or the nitrogen light. That plain fact, Heath argues, proves the glow is lit by particles bumping into each other. He then matches the brightness he saw against values worked out from theory. For the oxygen glow, the match is excellent, he reports.
the-tryal-of-william-penn-william-mead-f:
The Tryal of William Penn and William Mead concerns a tumult at the Old Bailey in September 1670. It is transcribed here from the Compleat Collection of State Tryals. That collection was first published in 1719, and this edition is by Don C. Seitz. His foreword declares that liberty, equality, and fraternity were preached through all time. Yet William Penn, the Quaker, came nearer establishing that trinity than any other human before or since. The edition is dedicated to the memory of Thomas Jefferson, 'which needs frequent refreshing.'

Penn and Mead were tried for preaching to a London crowd after their meeting house was shut. The jury's refusal to convict became a landmark of jury independence. The defendants published the account themselves, as the title page proudly says, 'Done by Themselves.' Readers get a founding document of religious liberty in courtroom form.
theodore-roosevelt: Edmund Lester Pearson wrote a life of Theodore Roosevelt for the True Stories of Great Americans series, published by Macmillan in New York in 1920. A frontispiece photograph shows Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill, credited to Underwood and Underwood. Other Pearson titles are listed, from The Believing Years to The Librarian at Play. This record presents the title pages and that portrait only, so Pearson's biography itself is not shown here.
waltoniana-inedited-remains-in-verse-and: Richard Herne Shepherd edited Waltoniana, the unprinted remains in verse and prose of Izaak Walton. Walton wrote The Complete Angler. Shepherd issued the book at London in 1878, with his own notes and preface. Pages present here hold the title page, contents, and the first line of that preface only, so the remains themselves are not shown. The contents run by year from 1633 to 1683. They name an elegy on Dr. Donne and lines on Donne's portrait. Verses, an epitaph on Walton's second wife Anne Ken, and letters follow.
westerfelt:
Will N. Harben published the novel Westerfelt with Harper and Brothers in 1901. The story opens in a mountain home after a day of quilting. Two older sisters, Mrs. Slogan and Mrs. Dawson, have had neighbor women in to sew. They take the bright quilt from its frame as the sun goes down.

Harben draws the sisters with care, one sharp in speech and one softened by loss. Talk of fairs and rival quilts sets the local world in place. The scene gives readers a slow, warm start in a small rural town. Speech, work, and kin ties carry the early pages.
